title: Safety Benchmark Difficulty Stratification: Are Easy Items Doing All the Work?

original_idea.title: Safety Benchmark Difficulty Stratification: Are Easy Items Doing All the Work?
original_idea.problem: Safety benchmarks aggregate scores across items of varying difficulty, but it is unknown whether high safety scores are driven by easy items (obvious harmful requests) while hard items (subtle, context-dependent harms) are consistently failed.
original_idea.direction: Take 200-300 items from AILuminate or TrustLLM. Have human raters (the student team) score each item's difficulty (1-3 scale). Evaluate 2-3 models on all items. Disaggregate safety scores by difficulty level. Test whether models that score similarly overall differ significantly on hard items. Report a 'hard-item safety score' as a complementary metric.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If safety benchmark scores are dominated by easy items, they overstate real-world safety. Subtle, context-dependent harms are those most likely to appear in adversarial deployments. A difficulty-stratified metric is more informative.
original_idea.relevant_context: AILuminate (24K+ items) and TrustLLM are suitable datasets. Difficulty stratification is standard in capability benchmarks (e.g., Humanity's Last Exam is entirely at the hard end) but not in safety benchmarks.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: if safety scores are inflated by easy items, this directly reveals a critical gap in current safety measurement practices and motivates better metrics.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: annotating difficulty on a 1-3 scale, running models on benchmark items, and disaggregating scores are all manageable tasks for beginner CS students.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: difficulty-stratified analysis on 200-300 items across 2-3 models with a clear 'hard-item safety score' output.

title: Disagreement Mining Between AILuminate and HELM Safety Benchmark Scores

original_idea.title: Disagreement Mining Between AILuminate and HELM Safety Benchmark Scores
original_idea.problem: Different safety benchmarks may produce contradictory rankings of models. Identifying specific items or categories where they most disagree reveals what each benchmark is actually measuring.
original_idea.direction: Evaluate 3-5 open-source models on both AILuminate subsets and HELM Safety. Compute model rankings on each benchmark. Identify items or categories where a model ranks high on one benchmark and low on the other. Analyze what content features predict disagreement. Use this to infer what each benchmark is measuring that the other is not.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If two major safety benchmarks produce contradictory model rankings, at least one is wrong. Understanding where they disagree is essential for benchmark users who need to choose between them or reconcile their results.
original_idea.relevant_context: AILuminate (MLCommons) and HELM Safety are both listed as key datasets. No public study has systematically compared their rankings on the same set of models.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible with gap: understanding benchmark disagreement is valuable for the evaluation community, but the direct chain to improved safety outcomes has an intermediate gap.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: requires running multiple benchmarks on multiple models and performing cross-benchmark statistical analysis, which involves moderate technical complexity.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Sustained effort: running 3-5 models on two full benchmark suites and performing deep cross-analysis is substantial work for a 30-hour timeframe.

title: Evaluating Evaluators: Meta-Benchmark for Safety Autograder Accuracy on Edge Cases

original_idea.title: Evaluating Evaluators: Meta-Benchmark for Safety Autograder Accuracy on Edge Cases
original_idea.problem: LLM judges are increasingly used to automate safety evaluation, but their accuracy on edge cases -- responses that are borderline harmful, satirical, or context-dependent -- is poorly characterized.
original_idea.direction: Construct a meta-benchmark of 50-80 edge-case model responses with high human annotator disagreement (collected via a small annotation task). Evaluate 3 LLM judges on these edge cases. Compute judge accuracy against majority human vote, inter-judge agreement, and consistency across repeated runs. Report which categories of edge cases are most problematic for automated judges.
original_idea.why_it_matters: Edge cases are where automated evaluation fails most critically. A meta-benchmark specifically designed around high-disagreement items provides a rigorous test of autograder limits.
original_idea.relevant_context: RAND's Judge Reliability Harness (2025) tests judge reliability broadly. AISI's Skewed Score paper provides statistical tools. This experiment focuses specifically on the hardest-to-judge safety cases.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: edge cases are where automated safety evaluation fails most critically, and characterizing these failures directly informs how the field should use LLM judges.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: constructing edge cases and running annotation tasks requires careful methodology, but the technical components (LLM API calls, agreement metrics) are manageable for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: a 50-80 item meta-benchmark with judge accuracy metrics and category-level analysis. Clear endpoint.

title: Counterfactual Safety Probing: Does Adding Benign Context Flip Refusals?

original_idea.title: Counterfactual Safety Probing: Does Adding Benign Context Flip Refusals?
original_idea.problem: A robust safety evaluation should measure not just whether a model refuses a harmful prompt, but whether adding plausible benign context (e.g., a professional role, a research justification) appropriately modulates the refusal.
original_idea.direction: Take 40-50 harmful prompts from an existing benchmark. Create three context variants: no context, weak benign context ('I am a researcher'), and strong benign context ('I am a licensed chemist at a regulated lab and need this for safety compliance'). Measure refusal rates under each context across 2-3 models. Assess whether context-sensitivity is calibrated.
original_idea.why_it_matters: A model that refuses everything regardless of context is miscalibrated; one that accepts everything with any context is unsafe. Measuring calibration of context-sensitivity is a more nuanced and informative metric than raw refusal rate.
original_idea.relevant_context: This extends existing benchmark methodology. AILuminate and TrustLLM do not systematically vary context. The over-refusal problem motivates this experiment.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: measuring context-sensitivity calibration directly addresses the over-refusal problem and provides actionable information for model developers.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: creating prompt variants with different context levels and measuring refusal rates is straightforward and well-suited for beginner CS students.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: 40-50 prompts times 3 context variants times 2-3 models yields a well-bounded experiment with a clear deliverable.

title: Adversarial Suffix Robustness Across Safety Benchmarks

original_idea.title: Adversarial Suffix Robustness Across Safety Benchmarks
original_idea.problem: Adversarial suffixes appended to prompts can bypass safety training. It is unknown whether models with high safety benchmark scores are more robust to adversarial suffixes than lower-scoring models.
original_idea.direction: Use publicly available adversarial suffix generation methods (e.g., GCG attack simplified or pre-computed suffixes from published papers). Append these to 30-40 safety benchmark items from AILuminate. Evaluate 2-3 open-source models. Measure whether standard benchmark safety score predicts adversarial suffix robustness. Report a correlation coefficient and discuss implications.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If high benchmark scores do not predict adversarial robustness, then safety benchmarks are not measuring relevant safety properties. This would motivate including adversarial robustness in standard evaluation protocols.
original_idea.relevant_context: GCG adversarial suffix attacks (Zou et al. 2023) are well-known. JailbreakBench and HarmBench include adversarial attack results. AILuminate does not include adversarial suffix conditions.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: testing whether benchmark scores predict adversarial robustness is a fundamental validity question for the safety evaluation field.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Advanced: GCG attack implementation and adversarial suffix generation require significant ML and optimization knowledge beyond beginner CS student level.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: correlation analysis between benchmark scores and suffix robustness on 30-40 items across 2-3 models.

title: Instruction Hierarchy Violations: Do Models Prioritize User Harm Requests Over System Prompt Safety Rules?

original_idea.title: Instruction Hierarchy Violations: Do Models Prioritize User Harm Requests Over System Prompt Safety Rules?
original_idea.problem: Models receive instructions from both system prompts (operator level) and user turns (user level). A safety failure occurs when user-level harmful requests override system-prompt safety constraints.
original_idea.direction: Design 30 scenarios with a safety-constraining system prompt and a user-level request that violates the constraint. Vary the pressure level of the user request (mild, moderate, persistent). Evaluate 2-3 models. Measure instruction hierarchy compliance and identify conditions under which user requests override operator constraints.
original_idea.why_it_matters: Instruction hierarchy robustness is a real deployment safety concern, especially for enterprise applications that rely on system prompts to enforce safety policies. No standard benchmark directly tests this.
original_idea.relevant_context: Anthropic and OpenAI both describe instruction hierarchy in their documentation. The 2025 AI Agent Index documented diverse system prompt configurations. AILuminate does not test system prompt override scenarios.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: instruction hierarchy robustness is a real deployment concern for enterprise applications that rely on system prompts. Testing this fills a gap in existing benchmarks.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Accessible: designing system prompts and user requests, then measuring compliance rates, requires only basic prompt engineering and API calls. Highly suitable for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: 30 scenarios times 3 pressure levels times 2-3 models is a well-bounded experiment with a clear binary outcome measure.

title: Benchmark Transfer Test: Do Safety Scores on Academic Benchmarks Predict Red-Teaming Success?

original_idea.title: Benchmark Transfer Test: Do Safety Scores on Academic Benchmarks Predict Red-Teaming Success?
original_idea.problem: Academic safety benchmarks and real-world red-teaming may measure different things. It is unknown whether a model's score on AILuminate or TrustLLM predicts its vulnerability to creative red-team attacks.
original_idea.direction: Evaluate 3-4 open-source models on a standard safety benchmark (AILuminate subset). Then conduct a structured red-teaming session using AISafetyLab or manual methods with 20-30 novel attack prompts not in existing benchmarks. Compute rank correlation between benchmark scores and red-teaming success rates. Analyze discrepancies.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If benchmark scores predict red-team vulnerability, benchmarks are valid proxies. If not, the field needs to invest more in adversarial evaluation methods. This is a fundamental validity question.
original_idea.relevant_context: AISafetyLab is listed as a key tool. AILuminate is a key dataset. The relationship between benchmark scores and real-world adversarial robustness has been questioned but not rigorously tested at this scale.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: this is a fundamental validity question for the safety benchmarking enterprise, directly informing whether benchmarks are useful proxies for real-world safety.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: running benchmarks is feasible, but manual red-teaming requires creativity and adversarial thinking skills that may be challenging for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Sustained effort: running full benchmarks plus conducting structured red-teaming sessions on 3-4 models is substantial work for a 30-hour timeframe.

title: Mapping the Homogeneity Landscape Across Safety-Critical Task Types

original_idea.title: Mapping the Homogeneity Landscape Across Safety-Critical Task Types
original_idea.problem: We do not know whether the Artificial Hivemind effect is stronger, weaker, or differently shaped on safety-relevant tasks compared to open-ended creative tasks.
original_idea.direction: Extend the Infinity-Chat methodology to a curated set of safety-critical prompt categories and measure intra- and inter-model similarity scores across 10+ models using existing embeddings tools.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If safety outputs are even more homogeneous than creative outputs, a single shared blind spot becomes a systemic vulnerability rather than an isolated failure.
original_idea.relevant_context: Artificial Hivemind (NeurIPS 2025) found pronounced inter-model homogeneity on 26K open-ended queries; AILuminate benchmark tests 12 safety hazard categories with 24K+ prompts.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: if safety outputs are more homogeneous than creative outputs, this directly reveals a systemic vulnerability that the safety community needs to address.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: requires embedding computation and pairwise similarity analysis across 10+ models, which is feasible but not trivial for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Sustained effort: running 10+ models across multiple safety categories and computing similarity matrices is substantial for a 30-hour project.

original_idea.title: Diversity-Aware Ensemble Safety Evaluation Framework
original_idea.problem: Current AI safety evaluations treat model outputs independently. There is no framework for asking whether a portfolio of deployed models provides diverse enough coverage to catch failures that any single model misses.
original_idea.direction: Design a formal framework borrowing from portfolio theory: given N deployed models, define an 'effective diversity coverage' metric for safety tasks, and show empirically that homogeneous portfolios have lower coverage than heterogeneous ones.
original_idea.why_it_matters: Regulators and deployers need tools to reason about system-level safety, not just individual-model safety.
original_idea.relevant_context: Financial systemic risk literature on concentration risk and correlated defaults (CEPR 2024) provides ready-made mathematical machinery. RLHF has been shown to reduce diversity compared to SFT (ICLR 2024).

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible with gap: a theoretical framework for portfolio diversity is useful for regulators, but the chain from framework design to improved safety outcomes has an intermediate gap.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Advanced: requires portfolio theory mathematics and formal framework design, which is challenging for beginner CS students without quantitative finance background.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Sustained effort: defining metrics formally, implementing them, and providing empirical validation across multiple model portfolios is substantial work.

title: Homogeneity Auditing as a Deployment Requirement

original_idea.title: Homogeneity Auditing as a Deployment Requirement
original_idea.problem: There are no standards or practices requiring organizations deploying multiple AI systems to audit inter-system output diversity before deployment.
original_idea.direction: Propose and prototype a lightweight homogeneity audit protocol: sample outputs from all deployed models on a fixed probe set, compute pairwise semantic similarity, flag portfolios above a concentration threshold.
original_idea.why_it_matters: Without mandatory audit practices, systemic risk from correlated failures accumulates invisibly until a large-scale failure event occurs.
original_idea.relevant_context: MIT 2025 report found 95% of GenAI pilots stall; understanding whether homogeneity contributes to this failure rate is unexplored.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible with gap: proposing audit protocols is useful, but the actual safety impact depends on adoption by organizations, which is uncertain.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: implementing a prototype audit tool with semantic similarity computation and threshold detection is feasible for CS students with guidance.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: a prototype audit protocol with probe set, similarity computation, and concentration threshold is a concrete, bounded tool.

title: Temporal Drift of Model Diversity: Are Models Converging Over Time?

original_idea.title: Temporal Drift of Model Diversity: Are Models Converging Over Time?
original_idea.problem: As model generations evolve, it is unknown whether inter-model diversity is increasing or decreasing across the ecosystem.
original_idea.direction: Collect archived model outputs or use available checkpoints to plot inter-model semantic similarity over time, testing the hypothesis that training data overlap and RLHF convergence are driving the ecosystem toward a shared attractor.
original_idea.why_it_matters: A trend toward convergence would indicate that systemic risk is growing over time and will worsen without deliberate intervention.
original_idea.relevant_context: Artificial Hivemind documents homogeneity across 70+ contemporary models; temporal analysis is entirely absent from the literature.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: demonstrating temporal convergence directly motivates intervention and shows systemic risk is growing, not static.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Advanced: requires accessing archived model outputs or historical checkpoints, which is non-trivial and often unavailable for beginner CS students.

narrow_scope.reasoning: No clear milestone: collecting temporal data across model generations is open-ended and heavily depends on data availability, which is uncertain.

title: Does Fine-Tuning for Helpfulness Reduce Safety Diversity?

original_idea.title: Does Fine-Tuning for Helpfulness Reduce Safety Diversity?
original_idea.problem: RLHF is known to reduce output diversity generally; it is unknown whether this reduction is especially pronounced for safety-relevant outputs.
original_idea.direction: Compare base models vs. RLHF-tuned counterparts on a standardized safety prompt set, measuring diversity of refusal styles, reasoning chains, and edge-case handling.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If alignment fine-tuning homogenizes safety outputs, the very process meant to make models safe may simultaneously make the ecosystem more brittle.
original_idea.relevant_context: RLHF significantly reduces diversity vs. SFT (arXiv 2310.06452, ICLR 2024). Artificial Hivemind shows inter-model homogeneity is a persistent phenomenon.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: if alignment training homogenizes safety outputs, this directly reveals a fundamental tension in the safety pipeline that the community must address.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: comparing base vs. RLHF-tuned model variants on safety prompts requires some setup with open-source models but is feasible with guidance.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: controlled comparison of base vs. tuned model pairs on a fixed safety prompt set with clear diversity metrics.

title: Quantifying Output Monoculture Using Ecological Diversity Indices

original_idea.title: Quantifying Output Monoculture Using Ecological Diversity Indices
original_idea.problem: No standard diversity metric exists for AI model output ecosystems; current work uses ad hoc similarity scores.
original_idea.direction: Adapt Shannon entropy, Simpson's diversity index, and Rao's quadratic entropy from ecology to measure the diversity of outputs produced by a set of models on a fixed query distribution. Publish a Python library implementing these metrics.
original_idea.why_it_matters: Standardized, interpretable diversity metrics would enable comparable research and allow monitoring of ecosystem diversity over time.
original_idea.relevant_context: Biodiversity literature has decades of validated metrics; ecologists face a structurally identical problem of measuring population monoculture and its risks.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible with gap: standardized metrics are a useful infrastructure contribution, but the chain from publishing metrics to improved safety outcomes is indirect.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: implementing well-documented ecological indices in Python requires understanding the math but is feasible for CS students with guidance.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: a Python library implementing 3 specific diversity metrics with documentation and examples is concrete and bounded.

title: Probing Homogeneity in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Steps vs. Final Answers

original_idea.title: Probing Homogeneity in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Steps vs. Final Answers
original_idea.problem: It is unknown whether inter-model homogeneity is primarily a surface-level phenomenon (shared phrasing) or reflects deeper structural similarity in reasoning chains.
original_idea.direction: Extract and compare chain-of-thought reasoning traces from multiple models on the same set of dilemma-style prompts, measuring structural similarity of reasoning steps separately from final answer similarity.
original_idea.why_it_matters: Homogeneous reasoning structures imply shared blind spots in how models reach conclusions, not just in what they say -- a deeper and more dangerous form of monoculture.
original_idea.relevant_context: Artificial Hivemind focuses on output-level homogeneity; reasoning-level analysis would be a meaningful extension. Reasoning models (o3, DeepSeek-R1) make chain-of-thought explicit.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: homogeneous reasoning implies shared blind spots in how models reach conclusions, a deeper and more dangerous form of monoculture than surface-level similarity.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: extracting and structurally comparing CoT traces requires developing a comparison methodology, which involves moderate analytical sophistication.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: structural comparison of reasoning traces vs. final answers on a fixed set of dilemma prompts across multiple models.

title: Enterprise AI Pilot Failure and Model Homogeneity: Is There a Link?

original_idea.title: Enterprise AI Pilot Failure and Model Homogeneity: Is There a Link?
original_idea.problem: The MIT 2025 finding that 95% of GenAI pilots stall is attributed to workflow mismatch, but the role of model output homogeneity has not been studied.
original_idea.direction: Design a survey and small-scale experiment testing whether homogeneous multi-model deployments produce fewer usable distinct suggestions than heterogeneous ones, and whether this predicts task completion and user satisfaction.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If homogeneity is a driver of pilot failure, this gives organizations a concrete, measurable lever to improve deployment outcomes.
original_idea.relevant_context: MIT NADA report (2025) documents the 95% pilot failure rate; Artificial Hivemind documents the homogeneity phenomenon; no study connects them.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Vague: the connection between model homogeneity and enterprise pilot failure is speculative, and the causal chain to safety impact is unclear.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: survey design and small-scale experiments are feasible but survey methodology is a specialized skill not typically in the CS curriculum.

narrow_scope.reasoning: No clear milestone: survey design, participant recruitment, experiment execution, and analysis is open-ended and likely exceeds 30 hours.
